title: Introduce memory leak
description: Project: Introduce memory leak. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: Memory leaks in managed applications are subtle. The process does not crash; it grows. Over hours or days, working set climbs until the operating system starts paging, garbage collection pauses lengthen, and the process is eventually recycled. This lesson introduces how .NET memory leaks happen, how to detect them with production diagnostics, and how to fix the most common patterns.

items: Event handlers are subscribed but never unsubscribed, keeping the publisher alive indefinitely
Cached objects in static dictionaries or memory cache without eviction policies
Large object heap fragmentation when byte arrays or strings are allocated and discarded frequently
Unmanaged resources held by managed wrappers without explicit Dispose calls
Captured closures in LINQ or async lambdas that reference entire parent scopes
Diagnostic or logging buffers that grow unbounded under error storms

terms.definition: The automatic memory manager in .NET that reclaims memory from objects no longer reachable from GC roots.
A separate heap for objects larger than 85,000 bytes that are collected less frequently and not compacted by default.
A reference that keeps an object alive, including static fields, thread stacks, and pinned handles.
A protocol for releasing unmanaged resources deterministically before garbage collection reclaims the wrapper object.
A reference that does not prevent the referenced object from being collected, useful for caches that should not extend object lifetime.

data.text: The most common leak in ASP.NET Core applications is an event subscription that outlives its subscriber. When a hosted service subscribes to an event on a singleton, and the subscriber is scoped or transient, the subscriber will never be collected because the singleton holds a delegate reference to it. This is invisible until you look at memory dumps or profiling data.

items: Monitor working set and private memory in production with dotnet-counters or /diagnostics
Capture memory dumps with dotnet-dump when memory exceeds expected thresholds
Use PerfView or dotMemory to view object retention graphs and find GC roots
Compare generation 0, 1, and 2 collection counts to identify objects surviving too long
Review event handler registrations and static collections in suspect modules

data.title: Use WeakReference for caches
data.text: If you must cache objects in a static collection, consider whether the cache should extend their lifetime at all. A MemoryCache with size limits and eviction policies is almost always safer than a raw Dictionary<TKey, TValue> that grows forever.

items.question: How do I confirm a leak without a profiler?
items.answer: Record dotnet-counters over several hours and plot the Gen 2 heap size. A steadily climbing Gen 2 heap with no corresponding drop after a forced full GC indicates objects are being rooted. Combine this with a production memory dump for the exact types.

items.question: Can garbage collection cause memory leaks?
items.answer: GC only reclaims unreachable objects. If a reachable object holds references to many others, GC cannot collect them. The leak is in the object graph, not in GC itself.

items.question: Should I disable server GC for debugging?
items.answer: Server GC can make memory dumps larger and harder to interpret because each thread has its own heap. Disable it temporarily for simpler heap analysis, but always test fixes with server GC enabled.

data.title: Find the leak in a hosted service
data.description: You receive a memory dump from an ASP.NET Core service that has been running for three days. The working set is 4 GB but the application should need only 200 MB. Using PerfView or dotMemory, identify the type that dominates the heap and explain why it is rooted.
steps: Open the dump in a profiler and view the dominated-by-size view
Identify the top object type and its retained size
Inspect the path to the GC root
Propose a code fix based on the root type
data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to describe the leak mechanism in one or two sentences and propose a concrete code or configuration fix.

data.title: Summary
points: Memory leaks grow working set without crashing; monitor both metrics
Event handler leaks are the most common pattern in .NET services
Capture production dumps; dev-only profiling misses production data shapes
Use GC root analysis to find who is holding references
Prefer bounded caches and deterministic disposal over unbounded collections
data.takeaway: Treat unbounded growth as an incident even when the process has not crashed. The cost of investigation is far lower than the cost of an emergency restart during peak traffic.
